To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

a) a software implementation of the data whitening routine of the DES is vulnerable to first order DPA; b) the data whitening implementation can be modified to resist a first order DPA by adding a small amount of hardware (e.g. a 4-bit adder); c) the modified implementation is vulnerable to a second-order DPA; d) the second order DPA can be optimized by using a simple power leakage function that is based on Hamming Weight; and e)

1) a software implementation of the whitening routine is vulnerable to both a first order and a second order DPPA attack; 2) the first order DPPA resistance is achieved by using the same key for both the whitening and the decryption routines, while the second order DPPAs is resisted by using a different key for the whitening and for the decryption routines; 3) the optimal second order DPPAA attack requires the knowledge of the whitening key, and

(1) a software implementation of an AES whitening routine is vulnerable to a first and second order Differential Power Analysis; (2) a first order DPA-resistant whitening routine is not resistant to a second order attack; (3) a second order DSA is proposed that is optimal under the assumption of independent and identical distributions of the Hamming weights; and (4) the second order attack is shown to be feasible on an AES whitening algorithm implemented on an ST16 smart card.
In summary, our research is concerned with
a second order DDA attack on a software implementation of the AES.
the security of software implementations of cryptographic primitives against DPA attacks.
the following question: "Can the security of a cryptographic algorithm be improved by modifying the software implementation of the algorithm?".
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the second order power analysis is a more serious threat to the security of smartcards than the first order power analysis, and the second order power attack is more practical than the first order attack.
the second order DPA is the most powerful attack against a data whitening algorithm.
a second order DDA (differential power analysis) attack can be performed against the whitening routine, but that a second order attack is not necessarily the best attack to use.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

second order DPA is a serious threat to the security of smartcards, and that the security of software implementations of cryptographic algorithms can be improved by using the second order DPA as a threat model.
a software implementation of data whitening routine can be vulnerable to a DPA attack if the power consumption of the device is not well understood.
the DPA resistant software implementation is not resistant enough.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the use of a second order DPD attack is not only a valid threat, but is also a viable option to attack software implementations of data whitening routines.
a DPA resistant software implementation may be vulnerable to a higher order DPA attack if the implementation is not carefully designed.
the Hamming weight leakage model is a good approximation for the power consumption of software running on a smartcard and can be used to perform a second order DSA attack.
